It could be vastly underestimated how much human expertise is needed to diffuse the benefits of AI to the long-tail of knowledge work. I think more data companies should figure out this branding, where experts help AI companies understand how to improve the tools that make them more effective, rather than replaced.

Some jobs will be replaced for sure, but I think a lot of knowledge work is deeply interpersonal, messy, and context driven in a way where AI adoption will be a productivity boon to existing employees. We are seeing this with the demand for SWEs today.

This rebrand will serve the AI industry writ large very well, but goes against the RSI narratives of the labs as "ASI will replace all knowledge work." In some ways, the difference is more philosophical about "what is the nature of work." I believe knowledge work is much more human than the evals give credit for, and this will make diffusion take a long time. Seems like Mercor can be at the center of this diffusion puzzle.

Disclosure: Yes, I advise Mercor on trying to realize this puzzle, as I think it's super interesting.

I welcome the leadership of President @EmmanuelMacron, who brought together heads of government, leaders of frontier AI companies, and international researchers today to discuss the growing risks of advanced AI, including dangerous loss of control and misuse of AIs.

We must begin treating AI like other technologies which can deeply transform and threaten our societies: with intentional and rigorous governance frameworks. Model developers should undergo mandatory, independent audits by evaluators they do not choose, and be held accountable for demonstrating that their models are safe before they can pose a grave danger, a danger which can exist before their deployment.

Q: You spoke in your speech a lot about the core CPI print that's coming out today. That is a backward looking print. And I wondered how sensitive the committee were to the recent changes in the Brent price. We were at $118 per barrel a couple of weeks ago. When I left my desk this morning, we were $90.

Waller: The oil price will come back down, but I'm telling you diesel prices are not coming back down anytime soon. You don't have refining capacity. You're going to have a lot of oil sitting on ship somewhere, but it's not going to get processed into diesel anytime soon. That's what I mean by just because there's more oil coming out of the Gulf and barrels of oil price, it doesn't mean energy prices are necessarily going to drop in the near term for everybody else. I just don't see diesel coming down dramatically because more oil's coming out of the Gulf. You got to have refining capacity and that stuff's been seriously damaged around the world and isn't going to come back soon. So you can't just look at the price of a barrel of oil. Global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026. This is based on the latest preliminary estimates from the Global Carbon Project, published today.

This is a small reduction within an overall upward trend. Emissions have grown more slowly over the past decade than in previous decades, but they have not yet peaked or begun a consistent decline.

This fall mostly came from a reduction in oil consumption and a small decline in gas. Coal use increased slightly.

Among the major emitters, emissions are projected to fall in China, the United States, the European Union, and Japan. But they’re expected to increase by around 4% in India.

Why did emissions fall? The authors cite three key factors.

The deployment of clean energy (particularly solar and wind) displaced some fossil fuel use that would have otherwise been required to meet growing energy demand. Electric vehicles also reduced oil demand. Finally, the war in Iran and its impact on oil prices led to reduced demand, which has inadvertently reduced emissions.

Emissions from land-use change are more uncertain but are projected to increase this year due to peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia.

(written by @_HannahRitchie and Pablo Rosado)

We have updated our topic page on migration!

Hundreds of millions of people live in a country that is different from the one where they were born. In some countries, the majority of the population was born abroad.

International migration can affect both the countries people leave and move to. For example, remittances (money sent back to family or friends by immigrants) can be an important source of income in their country of origin. In destination countries, migration can fill employment and skills gaps and contribute to economic growth.

But migration is also among the top concerns for the public in many countries. In politics, it is often divisive and controversial. People are often concerned about the effects on jobs and employment, public services, crime, and local culture.

Understanding these benefits and challenges requires us to first have a clear picture of migration itself. This page provides a starting point, with writing, data, and visualizations on the global scale of international migration.

On this new version of our topic page, we first look at the types of migration people often think of when the term comes up: irregular or illegal migration. We move on to international migration overall: residents, annual flows, and the number of asylum seekers and refugees. We then look at the demographics of migrants and the scale of remittances — money migrants send to their countries of origin.

(This topic update was led by @_HannahRitchie, @EOrtizOspina, and Tuna Acisu.)

Launching @reificinc (backed by @ycombinator): RL environments for superhuman reasoning over time.

AI has learned to reason over text and code. But most of what matters in the real world shows up as numbers that change every second: a heartbeat, a bioreactor, a GPU cluster. No human can track thousands of signals at once, but AI should be able to.

In our environments, data streams in on a clock while the agent works, and every action is graded by what actually happened. Most AI training today teaches models to match human experts. We treat human performance as the floor.

Today, even the best frontier model averages under 50% on each of our three task families: personal agents, industry, and science & compute. Training an open model on our environments raised its full-solve rate on unseen tasks by 54% (from 25.6% to 39.5%), with no loss on general benchmarks.

I’m a published time-series researcher who simulated superconductors at CERN and shipped AI to hyperscalers as co-founder and CTO of Entangl (YC S24). I’ve seen firsthand how models that ace text and code fall apart on live signals, so I started Reific to build the infrastructure that keeps AI climbing the frontier, long past human level in the real world.

聊一聊《天道》丁元英原型，禅师李彪。

1969年，李彪出生在一个军人家庭，传闻他是某位上柱国的孙子，但他从未承认也从未否认。他的数学天赋极高，高中时参加全国数学竞赛拿了二等奖，大学直接进入数学系。

1992年深圳证券交易所刚成立一年，还在上大学的李彪在报纸上看到关于股票的报道，瞬间着了迷。他觉得股票这东西很有意思，K线图起伏的背后，是人性赤裸裸的博弈。

问题是李彪没钱，一个穷学生，哪来的本金炒股。他回了一趟家，找到父亲的一位老战友，看在他父亲的面子上，那位长辈借给他5万元。1992年北京房价每平米不到2000，一个普通工人月工资大概200元，5万元要不吃不喝攒20年。李彪揣着这5万块，踏上了开往深圳的火车。

时间来到1998年，此时的李彪已历经市场厮杀。他看上了业绩平平、长期在4到6元徘徊的冷门股“亿安科技”。在所有人看来这是支平庸的股票，但李彪认为它盘子小、流通市值低且股权分散，加上带有“科技”二字，是互联网泡沫前夕的绝佳炒作标的。

李彪花了半年时间极有耐心地建仓。他每天尾盘小单买入压制波动，让股价像死蛇一样在极窄区间横盘，以此消磨散户的耐心，在绝对低位尽可能多地收集筹码。  
筹码到手后，他祭出杀招：连续三个无征兆的跌停板砸下，让心存侥幸的技术派和散户在极致恐慌中割肉出局。第四天，巨量资金在跌停板悍然撬开封单上演地天板，一天之内从ICU冲进KTV，彻底洗净不坚定筹码。  
洗盘结束后，他开启了充满节奏感的拉升。从1999年初到5月将股价缓慢推升至15元，又经历5个月的横盘震荡折磨散户，逼走最后一批耐不住寂寞的人。  
1999年10月主升浪爆发，至2000年2月冲高至126.31元，创下A股首个百元股神话，涨幅超20倍。当市场疯狂喊着200元不是梦时，30岁的李彪在交易室里冷静地在高位放出各种利好，悄无声息地完成了出货。

亿安科技一战后，李彪在中国股市成为传奇，很多机构想高薪聘请他，很多老板想和他合作坐庄。但他决定退隐江湖，大隐隐于市，他在广州一个普通小区买了套房子，深居简出。邻居知道这个年轻人不用上班，整天在家对着电脑，却不知道他就是那个搅动股市风云的禅师。他觉得，钱赚够了，就该做点自己喜欢的事，资本市场就像赌场，玩久了，心就脏了，想清静清静。

2005年起，他在天涯论坛发帖，随后转战新浪博客改名“缠中说禅”，每天在家对着电脑更新文章，将孔子、老子、禅宗与诗词音乐融会贯通，系统阐述了名震后世的“缠论”。他的博客访问量突破1亿，每天有数十万股民守在电脑前等他更新。不仅如此，他还精准预言了2007年6124点的历史大顶及随后的暴跌，并提前预警了美国次贷危机引发的全球金融危机，让无数读者提前清仓躲过浩劫。

患病后，他在家里一边记录治疗过程，一边跟时间赛跑，在博客里写道：“本ID的理论，大概还需要三个月能全部写完，应该还来得及。”最终他在三个月内完成了最后的部分，在家中安然驾鹤西归，天妒英才。

据说，作家豆豆在17岁时结识李彪，被他的哲学思想和股市理念震撼。后来她以李彪为原型，创作了丁元英这个人物，写了一本小说《遥远的救世主》，改编成电视剧《天道》。丁元英的身上，有很多李彪的影子，大隐隐于市深居简出，股市鬼才，精通文化属性，看透人性本质。

回顾他的一生，无论是股市里冷血地看着散户割肉，还是后来隐居后对一切名利的淡漠，他始终用最绝对的理性践行着一个底层铁律：这世上从来没有什么救世主，也没有什么无缘无故的狗庄，市场里没有庄家只有输赢，如果你因为亏钱而怒骂庄家，那不过是因为自己又贪又怕却又想要结果，最终掉进了弱势文化的陷阱里。

多余的废话都是破绽，真正的高手从不预测未来，他们只是看透了规律，然后顺着规律，冷眼旁观地活成自己的神。

断轮刑是中世纪欧洲的招牌：人四肢摊开绑在车轮的辐条上，行刑人抡起包铁的木棍，隔着轮辐，一根一根敲断骨头
骨头断尽，再把轮子竖上高柱，人缠在轮子里示众，断气为止，快的一日，慢的两三日
🇫🇷 法国、🇩🇪 德国用它对付杀人越货的重犯，一用就是上千年
1762 年，图卢兹，新教商人让·卡拉斯被控杀害改宗天主教的长子，判了断轮
真相是长子自缢，但天主教占绝对多数的法庭认定：新教徒父亲容不下改宗的儿子
卡拉斯在轮子上被敲断四肢，高喊无罪，至死没有认罪
三年后，伏尔泰接手此案，写下《论宽容》，把审判的每一处荒唐摊在全欧洲面前
1765 年，巴黎高等法院为卡拉斯平反，国王出钱抚慰他的家人
断轮刑没有在那一年废除，它又苟延了二十多年
但从卡拉斯开始，欧洲人第一次大规模地意识到：杀人的不只是刑具，还有偏见
一个刑罚的终结，往往不是因为它太残忍
是因为它终于残忍错了人，而这次，有人替那个人把话说完了
——出处：法国图卢兹卡拉斯案档案；伏尔泰《论宽容》（1763 年）

同样一片汉中，魏延只用两万来人，依托外围关隘，稳稳守住四十四年。

到了姜维手里，曹魏十八万大军一到，短短三个月，汉中防线直接崩塌。

很多人说，是姜维改了祖宗留下来的防御法子，亲手拆掉了蜀汉的大门。这件事，到底该怎么看？

当年刘备拿下汉中，是他一生功业的顶峰。法正献策，抓住曹军主力东撤的机会，刘备凭坚壁相持耗走曹操，一举拿下汉中，还收下东三郡。

魏延就任汉中都督，定下一套思路：实兵诸围，御敌于外。

不在盆地里面消极死守，把兵力分散布置在秦岭各个谷口险要，卡住进山的通道。魏军千里而来，山路难走，粮草难继，只要关口啃不下来，久了自然退走。

这套打法，后来王平守兴势，用一万多兵力挡住曹爽十万大军，证明它确实可靠。

只是后来，荆州丢失、东三郡叛归魏国，汉中侧翼屏障消失，防御压力一下子重了很多。

诸葛亮时期，汉中变成北伐的前进基地；蒋琬、费祎主政，转向保守，不轻易大举出兵。费祎生前就劝姜维，不要寄希望一战定乾坤，先保境安民。

费祎遇刺之后，姜维终于放开手脚。在侯和一战败给邓艾之后，他在朝堂上也受到诸葛瞻、黄皓等人的排挤，于是远走沓中屯田。

也就是在这个阶段，他提出了一个颠覆性的方案：撤掉汉中外围的各个据点，收缩兵力，退守汉、乐二城，加上阳安关，坚壁积谷，放敌人进入汉中平原，再伺机截断粮道，把进来的魏军困死在盆地里。

这个方案，赢了就是惊艳的歼灭战，但它的容错率几乎为零。

263年，钟会大军直扑汉中，邓艾领兵牵制沓中的姜维。

外围据点已经撤空，魏军轻松进入盆地。

汉、乐二城闭门死守，可阳安关守将蒋舒临阵投降，关城粮仓、军备全部落入钟会手里，魏军直接就地补给，不用再千里运粮。

精心设计的诱敌计划，一个环节崩盘，全盘瓦解。

姜维千里回援，关口已经丢了，只能退到剑阁，死死挡住钟会主力。

谁也没料到，邓艾偷渡阴平，直插成都平原。刘禅一纸降书，蜀汉就此灭亡。

Commerce could have blocked chip shipments to Megaspeed the moment it found out that it was run by a Chinese spy, but it did not. Commerce has also refused to enforce regulations—which ironically remain on the books—that would require exporters to apply for a license to ship large numbers of AI chips to untrusted entities in many countries, which would prevent China from using shell companies like Megaspeed to buy controlled chips. Why is Commerce protecting Jensen and supporting his preferred policies even though it has known for months that Jensen was sleeping with a Chinese spy? Why is it STILL doing so?

Obviously Nvidia needs to take significant steps in its operations, security, and policy advocacy to ensure it takes national security concerns more seriously. What if immunosuppressive drugs could become tools to control therapeutic T cells rather than simply suppress them?

A major challenge in cell and gene therapy is the lack of clinically practical ways to selectively expand or eliminate engineered cells inside the body. This becomes particularly important when patients cannot discontinue immunosuppression, such as transplant recipients or individuals with immune dysregulation.

A new study introduces a multiplex prime-editing platform that turns commonly used immunosuppressive drugs into pathway-specific switches for controlling therapeutic T cells in vivo.

The investigators demonstrated several important applications:

Correcting pathogenic mutations: Prime editing corrected multiple immune dysregulation-associated variants in primary human T cells, including the HAVCR2 driver mutation in cells from patients with subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (SPTCL).

Selective expansion: Combining gene correction with drug-resistance editing enabled corrected SPTCL T cells to expand selectively under immunosuppressive pressure in humanized mouse models.

Reversible control: These engineered cells retained sensitivity to alternative agents, providing a potential mechanism for rapid in vivo suppression.

Broader applicability: Drug-resistant antigen-specific and CAR T cells maintained effector function despite pharmacologic immunosuppression.

Importantly, genomic, transcriptional, immunophenotypic, and clonal analyses demonstrated minimal off-target perturbation in the studied systems.

The implications extend beyond correcting inherited or acquired immune dysfunction. This strategy could help make CAR-T and other cellular therapies compatible with clinical settings in which immunosuppression is unavoidable.

The conceptual shift is significant: instead of asking patients to stop immunosuppression to protect therapeutic cells, we may be able to engineer therapeutic cells to function within—and be selectively controlled by—that immunosuppressive environment.

These remain preclinical findings, but they introduce a compelling framework for more controllable, adaptable cell therapies.

A point I emphasize again and again is that the relation between income and fertility is changing quickly, both within and between countries.

To make this point between countries, I take the total fertility rate (TFR) of up to 158 countries from the UN World Population Prospects and their GDP per capita from the Maddison Project, measured at purchasing power parity and in constant 2011 prices (that is, the data already correct for differences in price levels across countries and for inflation). I am not a big fan of the UN World Population Prospects, but this way nobody can accuse me of being selective with my sources.

Then I plot TFR against GDP per capita for 1950 (the start of the sample), 1985 (the midpoint of the sample), and 2022 (the last year in Maddison’s dataset).

The left panel includes all countries except the six Gulf oil exporters (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman), whose wealth comes from oil rents, not from their level of economic development. In the right panel, I also remove sub-Saharan Africa, a region with very poor data on TFR and GDP per capita.

Start with 1950 and 1985. Plot the two curves, and you will have trouble telling them apart. Countries with $2,000 of GDP per capita had 6.1 children per woman in 1950 and 5.9 in 1985. Countries with $5,000 had 4.3 in 1950 and 4.6 in 1985. Countries with $10,000 had 2.8 in both years. Countries got richer and had fewer children, but they moved down the same curve. In 1985, as in 1950, fertility dropped fastest between $5,000 and $10,000, and the typical country reached replacement (about 2.1 children per woman) only at around $14,000. Mexico, with $10,000 of GDP per capita, had 4.1 children per woman. Argentina, with $11,000, had 3.1.

And the relationship between TFR and GDP per capita held despite many other changes. For example, child mortality collapsed at every income level, literacy and life expectancy rose, again at every income level, modern contraceptive methods spread widely, and international organizations and local governments sponsored aggressive family-planning programs across Asia and Latin America from the 1960s. Nothing seemed to matter.

After 1985, the slope of the curve became much smaller (in absolute value) as the left end of the curve started falling quite fast while the right end of the curve barely changed. Interestingly, most of the fall came between 1985 and 1995, well before cell phones and social media (everyone’s favorite explanation) reached anyone outside a small elite of wealthy and highly educated persons.

At $2,000 of GDP per capita, fertility went from 5.9 children per woman in 1985 to 4.0 in 2022, a drop of 1.9 children. But at $20,000 of GDP per capita, fertility was 1.7 children per woman in 1985 and the same 1.7 in 2022.

Similarly, countries with 2.1 children per woman (roughly the replacement rate) were at $14,000 in 1985 but at $11,700 in 2022

Take Sri Lanka. Sri Lanka’s GDP per capita is $11,200, roughly the income at which the 2022 curve crosses replacement. According to the UN World Population Prospects, Sri Lanka has 2.0 children per woman in 2022, while the United States, with five times Sri Lanka’s income, has 1.7. The United States last had Sri Lanka’s income in 1923, when American women had about three children. And according to the most recent data from their national statistical agencies, Sri Lanka is in 2025 at 1.37 children per woman and the United States at 1.57. Sri Lanka has undershot American fertility by a considerable margin (yes, 1.37 is much lower than 1.57) a century before reaching American income.

I also decomposed the change in average TFR across countries into two parts. The first is the change from countries getting richer while moving along a fixed curve. The second is the change from the curve itself shifting, holding each country’s income fixed. 

From 1950 to 1985, almost all of the fall in TFR comes from countries getting richer. Remember: the curve barely moved. 

From 1985 to 2022, about 40% comes from countries getting richer and about 60% from the curve shifting down. That is the big surprise.

Is sub-Saharan Africa driving this result? Yes and no. In the right panel, we can see that the 1950 and 1985 curves barely change when we drop sub-Saharan Africa. Interestingly, the 2022 curve becomes almost flat. Outside sub-Saharan Africa, 92 of the 108 countries with more than $2,500 of GDP per capita have a TFR below 2.5. Most of the income gradient left in 2022 is an African gradient.

Why did the relation between TFR and GDP per capita hold for 35 years (in fact, for at least the early 1800s) and then fall? I do not have a proof, but my conjecture is that low fertility is driven not by income itself but by “modernity.” As I have explained in many posts, by “modernity” I mean the combination of phenomena such as large bureaucratic organizations, mass education, credentials, formal labor markets, and mass media. Until the 1980s, these features of modern life arrived together with economic development and high income. After 1990, the “modernity package” began to reach countries well ahead of income: secondary schooling for girls, television, and integration into global supply chains. Income stopped being a good proxy for “modernity,” so the curve drawn against income fell.

We are only beginning to glimpse the future of “modernity” without economic development. Mexico or Sri Lanka now have the fertility of Japan or Germany, but without the incomes of rich countries, without their state capability, and without their capacity to attract immigration. Becoming rich is no longer a precondition for having few children. Instead, for most of the planet, getting old before getting rich is the new normal.

Regional fertility differences in Switzerland since 1870:
In 1870, Switzerland already had one of the lowest TFRs in the World (only France had a lower TFR back then), but the regional differences weren't that big. Geneve had an extremely low TFR of 2.4 (replacement level was around 3.2).
By 1900, the regional differences got more pronounced and peaked in 1930. There was a strong urban/rural difference, but the Protestant/Catholic divide can clearly be seen as well, especially in French-speaking Switzerland, where Catholic Fribourg and Valais had more than double the TFR of the westernmost Protestant cantons.
The Baby Boom of the 1960s lifted the TFRs across the country, but the previous pattern remained mostly in place. In conservative and Catholic-majority central Switzerland, the TFR approached the levels of the American Baby Boom.
By 1990, the pattern changed somewhat to an urban/rural liberal/conservative divide. Appenzell-Innerrhoden, the last entity in the Western world to grant women's suffrage at the end of 1990, maintained the TFR levels of the Baby Boom until that year.
Nowadays, the TFR is low across Switzerland and regional differences have somewhat lost their importance.
